client: I've been really stressed out lately about school, specifically about my GPA. I got a lower grade than I expected on my last exam, and now I can't stop thinking about how it might ruin everything I've worked for. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the grade is already done and nothing can fix it now.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of worry right now, and that feeling of "everything I've worked for might fall apart" can be really heavy and consuming. I hear your skepticism about talking helping — and that's actually a really honest and understandable place to be when something feels so fixed and out of your control. I'm curious though: when you imagine this grade "ruining everything," what specific outcome are you most afraid of?

client: I think the thing I'm most scared of is that my GPA will drop enough that I lose my scholarship, and then I don't know how I'd even afford to stay in school. And beyond that, it's like... I've always been the person in my family who was supposed to "make it," and if I fail academically, I feel like I'm letting everyone down, not just myself. It's hard to even separate those two fears because they're all tangled up together.
therapist: That's such a meaningful thing to untangle — the financial fear is very real and concrete, but layered underneath it is this deeper weight of being the one who's "supposed to make it," which sounds like it's been something you've carried for a long time. It makes sense these feel inseparable, because one grade has somehow come to represent not just your GPA, but your whole identity and your family's hopes. I'd gently like to explore that second layer a bit — when you say you'd be "letting everyone down," do you know if that's something your family has actually expressed, or is it more a story you've been telling yourself?

client: Honestly, my family hasn't said it outright — like, nobody has sat me down and said "you better not fail or we'll be disappointed." But the message has always been kind of there in the background, like when my parents talk about me to relatives with so much pride, or when my mom mentions how much she sacrificed so I could have these opportunities. So I guess it is a story I'm telling myself, but it doesn't feel like just a story — it feels completely real and true.
therapist: It's really insightful that you can recognize it as a story you're telling yourself, even while it feels completely true — that tension is actually at the heart of a lot of the pressure we put on ourselves. The pride your family expresses and your mom's sacrifices are real, but somewhere along the way your mind has translated "they're proud of me" into "I must never fall short or I'll lose their love and respect," and those aren't actually the same thing. I wonder — if a close friend came to you with this exact situation, would you tell them that one difficult exam means they've failed the people who love them?

client: No, I would never say that to a friend — I'd probably tell them one exam doesn't define them and that they should just figure out how to do better next time. But when I try to apply that same logic to myself, it just doesn't stick the same way, like I know intellectually it's true but emotionally it feels completely different. I guess I hold myself to a standard I wouldn't hold anyone else to, and I'm not even sure why that is.
therapist: That gap between knowing something intellectually and actually *feeling* it is so common, and the fact that you can name it so clearly shows a lot of self-awareness. That double standard you hold for yourself — being so compassionate toward others but so unforgiving toward yourself — often has roots in something deeper, like a belief that your worth is tied to your performance in a way that other people's worth simply isn't. What do you think it would mean about you as a person, at your core, if you did fall short of this standard you've set?

client: I think at my core, if I fell short, it would mean I'm not actually as capable or special as everyone seems to think I am — like the whole image people have of me is a lie and I've just been faking it this whole time. There's this fear that if I slip up enough, people will finally see that I don't really belong here, that I got lucky or something. It's kind of exhausting to even say out loud because it sounds so dramatic, but that's genuinely what it feels like underneath all of it.
therapist: What you just described — that fear of being "found out" as not truly belonging — actually has a name, and it's called impostor syndrome, and it's incredibly common among people who are driven and high-achieving, so you're far from alone in this. It takes real courage to say it out loud, and it doesn't sound dramatic at all — it sounds like an exhausting secret you've been quietly carrying. I want to gently challenge one piece of it though: if you had truly been "faking it," what's the evidence that actually got you here — the scholarship, the academic path, all of it?

client: I mean, logically I know I worked hard to get here — I studied for countless hours, I earned the scholarship through my grades and an application process, it wasn't handed to me. But when I try to use that as evidence against the feeling, my brain just kind of... dismisses it, like it finds a way to say "yeah but that was then, and now you're slipping, so the truth is coming out." It's frustrating because I can see what you're doing and I understand the logic, but the feeling is so stubborn that the evidence doesn't really land the way it should.
therapist: That frustration you're feeling is actually really important information — your brain has essentially built a one-way filter where successes get explained away but struggles get treated as "the real truth," and that's a thinking pattern worth examining rather than just pushing more evidence against. The goal isn't to win an argument with that feeling using logic, because you're right that it doesn't work that way — it's more about slowly loosening the grip of that belief over time through experiences that contradict it. I'm curious: are there moments, even small ones, where you've felt genuinely competent or capable recently, where that "faking it" voice went quiet even briefly?

client: There was actually a moment a few weeks ago where a classmate asked me to explain a concept we were studying, and I was able to walk them through it clearly and they really got it — and in that moment I wasn't thinking about whether I belonged or not, I was just... doing it. But even as I say that now, part of me is already framing it as "well that was just one small thing, it doesn't count the same way a bad exam grade counts." I can hear how unfair that is, but I don't really know how to stop my brain from doing that automatically.
therapist: That moment with your classmate is actually a beautiful example of your real competence showing up naturally — and the fact that you can already hear how unfair it is that your brain discounts it tells me part of you *knows* the filter is broken, even if you can't switch it off yet. What you're describing is something we call a cognitive distortion — where your mind has different weights for negative and positive evidence, and the work is gradually teaching it to apply the same standard to both. It won't happen overnight, but I'd like to try something with you: what if, for the next week, you kept a small note of moments like that one — not to "win" against the impostor feeling, but just to start collecting evidence your brain currently throws away without examining?

client: I can see the logic in that, and part of me wants to try it, but I'm also a little worried that I'll either forget to do it in the middle of everything else going on, or that I'll do it and then still find ways to dismiss what I write down — like the same filter you're describing will just apply itself to the list too. I guess I'm also not sure a list of small moments is going to feel like enough to counteract something as big as a bad exam grade sitting right there in my transcript. Does this actually work for people, or does it just sound good in theory?
therapist: Your skepticism is completely valid, and honestly it's a sign of your intelligence that you can already see the potential pitfalls — this isn't blind resistance, it's thoughtful caution. To answer your question directly: yes, this does work for people, but not because a list magically overpowers bad feelings — it works slowly, because you're training your brain to *pause* before dismissing evidence, and that pause is where change actually happens. The filter you're worried about applying to the list is the same filter we're trying to loosen, so even noticing when you want to dismiss something you've written down is itself part of the work — would you be open to trying it as an experiment rather than a solution, just to see what comes up?

client: Framing it as an experiment rather than a solution actually does make it feel a little less pressured, like I don't have to prove it works or feel like a failure if it doesn't change everything immediately. I think I could try it, maybe just on my phone so it's easy to access — though I'm still a little nervous that the week I try this will be a week where nothing noteworthy happens and I end up staring at a blank list. I guess the honest answer is yes, I'm willing to try it, but I'm holding onto some doubt about whether I'll do it consistently or take it seriously enough to actually get anything out of it.
therapist: It's really encouraging that reframing it as an experiment gave you a little breathing room — that shift matters. The doubt you're holding onto isn't a problem to fix before you start; it's actually okay to begin with doubt, because the point isn't to feel certain, it's just to notice. And about the "blank week" worry — even a moment as quiet as finishing a difficult reading, or showing up to class when you didn't feel like it, counts as data worth writing down. What would feel like a realistic, low-pressure way to remind yourself to jot something down — maybe a small daily prompt on your phone?

client: Yeah, a daily reminder on my phone is probably the most realistic option for me — I already use it for everything else, so it wouldn't feel like adding some big new habit. Maybe something in the evening when I'm winding down, so I can look back at the day instead of trying to catch moments in real time. I think I can commit to that, even if some nights I open the reminder and genuinely struggle to think of anything to write down.
therapist: That sounds like a really solid, realistic plan — an evening wind-down check-in fits naturally into your day and gives you the perspective of looking back, which is actually more effective than trying to catch moments on the fly. On the nights where you open it and your mind feels blank, that's okay — even writing "I'm not sure what to put here" is still you showing up for yourself, which is itself something worth noting. As we wrap up today, I'm curious — how are you feeling now compared to when you first came in, a little skeptical that talking would change anything?
